articleTitle: Automatic number plate reading for transport applications
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Electronics in Managing the Demand for Road Capacity
abstract: Accident rates remain high for some roads. In many of the instances excess speed was a contributing factor and, consistent with established theories, evidence suggests that the excessive speed increased the level of injury. The role that technology can play in the development and trial of a speed detection and deterrent system which automatically reads vehicle registration plates and displays those exceeding the speed threshold, together with the recorded speed, on a variable message sign. The system has become known as SVDD. (Speed Violation Detection Deterrent).<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Pricing general road usage using vehicle borne electronics
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Electronics in Managing the Demand for Road Capacity
abstract: In developing a system to charge for road usage, especially in cities, the author considers a complex pattern of existing use and freedom of travel which the roaduser currently enjoys. To make any system of charging politically acceptable it must be seen to be reasonable by both those who would pay and those who decide to impose it. The article considers the subject of charging for motorway use as a simpler issue in all respects than one concerning urban charging, so thinking has concentrated on urban issues rather than inter-urban ones.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Digital CCTV processing in traffic management
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Electronics in Managing the Demand for Road Capacity
abstract: Image processing is becoming an attractive option for a range of traffic management applications, where previously they would not have been considered on cost-benefit grounds. To date, applications of image processing have been mostly limited to freeway locations and urban areas where CCTV is already in place or is planned. With the advent of the first production samples of cameras 'on a chip', image processing could be on the threshold of a significant breakthrough in functional capability. The paper focuses on the development of a specific platform which is intended to address current traffic management applications.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Electronics in Managing the Demand for Road Capacity
abstract: ROMANSE is a three year Pounds 8.5 million pilot project based in Southampton and led by Hampshire County Council. It forms part of the DRIVE 2 project SCOPE which also embraces the cities of Cologne in Germany and Piraeus in Greece. The main objectives are to influence travel behaviour by the dissemination of accurate, timely traffic and travel information. As a result, it is hoped to increase demand for public transport, improve network efficiency as a whole and provide high quality data for immediate and long-term strategic decisions. These objectives will be achieved through the formation of a Traffic and Travel Information Centre (TTIC). This will collate, evaluate, coordinate, and disseminate real-time and forecast information on transport networks and service conditions for all modes of transport. In doing this, ROMANSE will influence a number of factors, including the decision as to whether to undertaken or abandon a trip, the mode of transport chosen, the time at which a trip is undertaken, the destination and the route taken.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: The specification of trip planning systems
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Electronics in Managing the Demand for Road Capacity
abstract: Trip planning systems are defined and research undertaken for the Science and Engineering Research Council (SERC) in determining such systems is outlined. The authors describe market research that was undertaken to determine the role for trip planning systems. They also describe work in testing proposed systems, through the development of a telephone computer prototype and a computer prototype.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Electronics in Managing the Demand for Road Capacity
abstract: It is possible to use fixed time UTC systems to restrict traffic but it is necessary to calculate the restraint timings by hand, an expensive procedure. However, within version 2.4 of SCOOT there is a facility to restrict traffic, the 'gating' facility, in response to demand on particular 'bottleneck' links within the controlled network. When the saturation on a bottleneck link rises above a threshold, then the green time is reduced on defined gated links. The gated links can be at some distance from the bottleneck; the first time that 'action at a distance' has been included in SCOOT. In fact the gated links can be anywhere in the controlled network, but stability problems are expected if they are a long way from the associated bottleneck.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Electronics in Managing the Demand for Road Capacity
abstract: Outlines the work being undertaken in Birmingham within the QUARTET project to develop, implement and test a range of measures to improve traffic and transport efficiency using Advanced Transport Telematics (ATTT) technologies, with the intention of integrating such measures and technologies where appropriate. Public transport has an important role to play in the future transport strategies of major cities affected by the impact of traffic growth and congestion, yet in the UK in particular there has been little investment in the sorts of high-tech management and information systems which has occurred elsewhere in Europe which help make public transport a viable alternative to the car. Moreover, deregulation of buses in the UK in 1986 created a whole new set of problems for bus users particularly that of obtaining accurate and up to date timetables. This paper illustrates some of the problems and the work being done in the Quartet and BLUEPRINT projects in Birmingham to secure improvements. QUARTET is being carried out in the cities of Athens, Birmingham, Stuttgart and Turin, with each city concentrating on particular aspects of ATT development. Birmingham (through Centro) is taking the lead in the area of public transport management and information systems: the ATT project in Birmingham is known as BLUEPRINT.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Design considerations for road-use pricing and automatic toll-collection systems
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Electronics in Managing the Demand for Road Capacity
abstract: The use of an automatic means of collecting revenue from a vehicle user for the use of road-space through road-use pricing or toll collection is one means of traffic demand management and is now being actively considered in the UK and throughout the world. Systems that currently exist to implement the automatic collection of road-use revenue are not particularly advanced and would not be suitable (in most cases) for large scale implementation. This paper describes the key issues and design considerations that need to be addressed in developing such a system, followed by a suggested implementation and suggested applications. Finally the paper describes an advanced transponder based debiting system which has been developed under the DRIVE II funded ADEPT (automatic debiting and electronic payment for transport) project which has been tackling and solving many of the highlighted problems with such systems. A description of the current ADEPT field trials (Cambridge, Lisbon, Goteborg, Thessaloniki and Trondheim) in automatic debiting and demand management is also presented.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: ROBIN-a MANNESMANN initiative for an innovative road pricing system
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Electronics in Managing the Demand for Road Capacity
abstract: A future road pricing system is expected to operate without any interference with the traffic flow, i.e. stopping at toll booths is inacceptable. Hence an electronic toll collection system is sought which neither requires special speed limits not lane restrictions at the point where the toll is raised. One should be able to install it on virtually all major European highways within a limited timeframe. Additionally several European countries have strict laws concerning the security and integrity of personal data, excluding registration of road users at the point of toll collection in a way which would allow a tracking of individuals. Existing road pricing schemes mostly rely on a communication between an in-car unit and some kind of fixed roadside beacons where the communication initiates the billing process and also serves for control purposes. The beacons are usually connected to a central computer. The installation of all the quite elaborate roadside equipment puts a heavy financial load on the road operator. A consortium within the Mannesmann group has proposed the Project ROBIN. The system fulfills all the above conditions without requiring any fixed roadside infrastructure, thus drastically lowering the initial investment necessary to install such a system. Additionally it can be gradually implemented for specific user groups, it can be made compatible to already existing toll collection systems, it can be quickly and flexibly adapted to any road network and it provides a maximum of personal data security and integrity.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Electronics in Managing the Demand for Road Capacity
abstract: Building on the finding that many travellers have difficulty in selecting the most efficient mode and route for a journey, interest has been shown in the development of advanced traveller information systems. Such systems could provide accurate and reliable information relating to the various options available for a journey, including public transport. This would enable the traveller to plan a journey on a fully informed basis. PROMISE is a development project within the EC DRIVE framework, that is addressing the provision of traveller information. The overall objective of the project is to develop and test a pan-European multi-modal traveller information system incorporating an open architecture and portable terminals. The PROMISE system will eventually provide a wide range of multi-modal traveller information services to the public.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Electronics in demand management-the working context
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Electronics in Managing the Demand for Road Capacity
abstract: Managing the demand for road capacity becomes necessary when the claims on highway space exceed the available supply. Successful demand management depends on the ability of traffic managers to influence the behaviour of potential and actual road-users. Thus, the introduction of transport electronics provides new means of achieving this behavioural modification. So far, development has been largely technology led and, as yet, there appears to be no generally accepted philosophy regarding the employment of the applications currently being introduced. In management terms, the advent of electronics constitutes a modern addition to a system which has evolved so as to control the operation of communications. However, unless one has a clear understanding of the operation of this present, substantially pre-electronic system, it is possible that some new initiatives could be inappropriate or even counter-productive. This paper is therefore offered as a contribution towards improving our understanding of the current situation.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Use of coordinated signal settings to reduce junction spill-back
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Electronics in Managing the Demand for Road Capacity
abstract: Situations in which a queue grows so as to block the entrance to the link at an upstream junction can cause various problems, including loss of junction capacity, increased driver stress and hazards to pedestrians crossing at the junction. In the worst case the spill-back may grow so as to produce grid-lock within a network. This paper describes word conducted in order to assess how the coordination of junction offsets in a congested network may help to minimise this disruption. A computer model was produced which used traditional speed-flow theory to represent traffic behaviour, eg traffic speeds, merging of traffic and queue evolution. Two test sites were selected for simulation purposes. The first is a three junction linear network whilst the second is a seven junction grid network. These simulation runs attempted to establish which stage at the upstream junction should be disrupted, given that spill-back was to occur. Results from a field trial on the linear network will be presented to show how the techniques can be applied on-street.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Automatic vehicle identification and its application to inter-urban road pricing
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Electronics in Managing the Demand for Road Capacity
abstract: In May 1992 the DART-Tag Automatic Vehicle Identification (AVI) system was launched at Dartford River Crossing for the nonstop cashless collection of tolls. This was the first full working system of electronic cashless toll collection in the UK and currently has in excess of 23000 users. The French manufacturer CSEE Peage, along with their UK subsidiary RTI Systems Ltd, saw their second major UK AVI toll collection system (FAST-Tag) launched in December 1992 at the Mersey Tunnels. It currently has over 13000 users. This paper discusses the requirements for remote identification systems and explains why microwave based techniques are best suited to AVI. A detailed description of DART-Tag follows, covering its lane equipment, computer system and associated real-time distributed database technology. Finally, recent developments in the application of AVI to a European inter-urban road pricing scheme are summarised.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>
